summary.text:
Wandsworth has no external debt at all. The last PWLB loan — the 2012 HRA subsidy buy-out — was repaid on 29 March 2025, and the General Fund has never borrowed. Against that it held £602.5m of investments at 30 September, and its adviser's April 2025 review placed it first for return out of 200 local authorities benchmarked.

The part that matters to the rest of the library is where the money goes. £235.0m, 39% of the portfolio, is out on short-term deposit with other councils at 4.88%, and the report says plainly why: local authorities are willing to borrow from them at significantly higher rates than banks. Appendix D puts a figure on the year before — one council paid 5.2% to borrow £10m for a year, with deposits peaking at 5.4%.

So Wandsworth is the counterparty on the other side of the short-dated inter-authority borrowing that Swale, Wiltshire, Cherwell, Herefordshire and Darlington are all paying for. Same market, seen from the lending side. They have also relaxed policy to lend to councils with modified audit opinions.

NOTE THE DATE: this is a mid-year paper at 30 September 2025, not the 2025/26 outturn.

officer.body:
Hi [OFFICER NAME],

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on the treasury update that went to Cabinet on 1 December, recognising that your 2025/26 annual report will have moved things on since. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it.

A scope note first, because it matters. What we hold is the mid-year paper at 30 September 2025, so everything below is on that date. If the annual report has restated any of it, that is our position being stale rather than yours being wrong.

We also hold no PWLB loans for Wandsworth, which is exactly what your paragraph 17 would predict — the 2012 HRA subsidy buy-out repaid on 29 March 2025 and nothing since. So the usual opening of this email, a loan-book reconciliation, has nothing to reconcile. That is not a common position and it is worth saying that your adviser's April review placing you first for return out of 200 authorities is consistent with everything in the paper.

The reason we wrote is the £235.0m. Thirty-nine per cent of your portfolio is out on short-term deposit with other local authorities at 4.88%, and Appendix A explains it: councils are willing to borrow from you at significantly higher rates than banks will pay. Appendix D puts a number on the year before — one council paying 5.2% to borrow £10m for a year, deposits peaking at 5.4%.

Here is why that is interesting to us and possibly to you. We read every council's treasury papers, and we have spent this summer reading the other side of your trades. Swale paying 6.25% for thirteen days over a year end. Wiltshire raising £100m from eleven authorities in four months at anything between 4.55% and 5.5%. Cherwell borrowing at 4.15% to 4.35% while lending at 6.42%. Herefordshire lending £5m each to Bexley and Newham at 7.00% for a month. Your own explanation of the cause — councils running down cash or borrowing short to avoid locking in PWLB rates — is exactly what those reports say from the borrower's side.

Nobody publishes this market. Every council sees its own trades and none sees the distribution, which is why the same week can produce 4.55% and 6.25%. As the largest lender into it that we have come across, you are the party with the most to gain from seeing the whole picture rather than the half you transact. We track inter-authority pricing across the sector alongside the PWLB curve, and July's PWLB lending was £368m across 33 loans from just 19 borrowers at an average 5.02% — thin PWLB months are precisely when councils come to you and the rate you can ask goes up. That breakdown is at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity.

Two other things. Your Appendix C change — lending to councils whose audit opinions are modified because of the audit backlog rather than anything about their finances — is a sensible distinction and one we have not seen another council spell out. It is also the kind of judgement that benefits from seeing how the sector as a whole is treating the same counterparties, which is what our LA credit work covers.

And the pooled funds. £130.0m of cost against £129.8m of value nets to almost nothing, but the spread underneath is wide — Fidelity Multi Asset Income at −15.0% and CCLA Property at −7.0% against Artemis at +20.7% and Royal London at +9.5%. Your decision to stop adding to multi-asset funds because of IFRS 9, while holding the existing ones under the override to 2029, is a clear position clearly explained, and the £8m volatility reserve behind it is more than most councils carry.

One small note of appreciation rather than correction: your paragraph 8 states the HRA preferential rate as 0.6% below standard, which is right. A surprising number of reports get that wrong or quote it against the certainty rate instead.

On training, four fit Wandsworth. Intra-LA borrowing & lending markets and LA Credit Analysis go to the £235m and the audit-opinion policy. Pooled funds (CCLA, multi-asset) and Financial instruments for treasury (IFRS 9) cover the other half. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
https://www.linkedin.com/in/russelltew

Source: Treasury Management update, Paper No. 25-419, Cabinet, 1 December 2025 (position at 30 September 2025).
